name: Governing AI in a Regulated Company
blurb: The policies and principles behind responsible adoption.
title: Governing AI in a Regulated Company
answer: Governance in life sciences starts from rules regulators have already set: the FDA and EMA principles of good AI practice, the FDA credibility framework for decision supporting AI, and the EU AI Act. A working governance model decides which data each tool may see, which decisions it may touch, and who approves new uses.

crumbs.name: AI Adoption and Governance in Life Sciences

reading.body:
Governance in life sciences starts from rules regulators have already set, not from internal policy invented in isolation. The FDA and EMA issued ten guiding principles of good AI practice in January 2026, and the FDA issued draft guidance on AI credibility for regulatory decision making in January 2025. The EU AI Act is the third external frame. A working model built on these decides which data each tool may see, which decisions it may touch, and who approves new uses.

The pattern is that the constraints arrive before the deployments. Two of the three governing documents are regulator-issued, and the FDA credibility framework is specifically about AI that supports decisions, which is where the risk sits in a regulated company. That shapes adoption more than model capability does. A tool that cannot show how it reached an output cannot support a regulatory decision, regardless of how well it performs.

For AI specifically, this pushes governance toward classification rather than prohibition. The practical instruction is to keep one register of AI uses, classify each by risk, and route high risk uses through quality and legal review before launch. That is an operational answer to a legal question, and it is the part a life sciences leader can act on.

What this does not cover is enforcement. The data names the principles, the credibility framework, and the Act, but records no penalty, no inspection finding, and no company that has been stopped. It also gives no count of how many firms have adopted such a register, so it cannot say whether this model is common practice or an aspiration.
